title: A Theory on Flow Matching with Neural Networks

paper.title: A Theory on Flow Matching with Neural Networks
paper.abstract: Abstract In this work, we develop theoretical foundation for flow matching with neural-network–parameterized conditional velocity fields. We establish convergence guarantees for gradient descent in the over-parameterized 2-layered ReLU neural network regime. We derive generalization bounds for the conditional velocity-field matching objective. Building on these results, we provide Wasserstein-distance guarantees for the samples generated by the induced flow. Our analysis is based on generalization bound for multi-task representation learning with unbounded losses, which may be of independent interest beyond flow-based generative modeling. These theoretical results are validated through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world image benchmarks.
paper.author_block: Yihan He Qishuo Yin Yuan Cao Jianqing Fan Han Liu

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2022 ) has emerged as a state-of-the-art approach within diffusion-based generative modeling for learning and sampling high-dimensional data, including images ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , and has been applied broadly across a range of other domains ( Lipman et al., 2024b ) . Flow matching is attractive in part because it cleanly separates three design choices: (i) the path of intermediate distributions (e.g., linear interpolation in data space / straight-line couplings in rectified flow ( Liu et al., 2022 ) , variance-preserving/variance-exploding diffusion schedules ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) , or transport maps motivated by optimal transport ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) ), (ii) the target velocity associated with that path ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) , and (iii) the numerical solver used at sampling time ( Chen et al., 2018 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . This modularity has led to a growing ecosystem of variants, including conditional flow matching constructions that leverage conditional distributions and couplings to define tractable target velocities ( Tong et al., 2024 ) . Empirically, these methods have been applied to high-dimensional generation tasks such as images, audio, and video ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Lipman et al., 2024a ; Guan et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2025 ) , and have also been used for conditional generation and editing, where one integrates an ODE while enforcing constraints (e.g., classifier guidance, inverse problems, or conditioning variables) ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Ho and Salimans, 2022 ; Song et al., 2022 ; Chung et al., 2023 ) . Beyond generation, learned continuous-time transports are increasingly used as primitives for data interpolation, domain translation, and simulation of complex dynamical systems ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Tong et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2018 ) . Despite this empirical success, a theoretical understanding of flow matching remains incomplete. There are three intertwined sources of error that ultimately determine the quality of generated samples: (1) optimization error from training neural networks with nonconvex objectives using first-order methods, (2) statistical error from learning the velocity field from finitely many samples, and (3) sampling error from approximating the continuous-time dynamics with a neural network learned velocity field. Hence, the questions that we address in this work can be summarized as follows: 1. What is the convergence guarantee for the neural network training with gradient descent ? 2. What is the generalization guarantee for the velocity field matching ? 3. What is the distributional guarantee for samples generated by neural-network-based flow matching?

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: To address the three questions above, we summarize our main contributions as follows. 1. We establish convergence guarantees for approximating high-dimensional conditional velocity fields using gradient-descent-trained two-layer neural networks. Our analysis connects the training dynamics to the neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime ( Du et al., 2018 ; Jacot et al., 2018 ) and addresses the challenges posed by high dimensionality, including regimes where the data dimension d d is of the same order as the sample size n n . 2. We derive L 2 L_{2} statistical error bounds for the velocity field learning problem by introducing a general high-dimensional multi-task learning generalization bound for unbounded losses. This result complements existing representation learning theory ( Maurer, 2016 ; Maurer et al., 2016 ) and may be of independent interest. 3. We provide sampling error guarantees for flow matching in Wasserstein distance. The proof combines a geometric lemma that upgrades L 1 L_{1} control to L ∞ L_{\infty} control on a compact high-dimensional subset with a refined analysis of the induced ODE dynamics. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first sampling error guarantee for gradient-descent-trained, neural-network-based flow matching algorithms. 4. Our theoretical results are complemented by numerical experiments on both the synthetic and real-world images that validate the convergence and sampling error bounds. These experiments provide insights into the practical implications of our theoretical findings and highlight potential avenues for future research.

sections.heading: Organization.
sections.text: The remainder of this work is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work and positions our contributions relative to existing literature. Section 3 introduces the main definitions and summarizes our results. Section 4 reports numerical experiments that complement the theoretical analysis. Finally, Section 5 discusses limitations and directions for future work.

sections.heading: 2 Related Works
sections.text: Our work is closely related to two branches of recent theoretical research on generative modeling and overparameterized neural networks. In the following, we first review recent theoretical developments for flow matching models, and then discuss the techniques most directly related to those used in this work.

sections.heading: Theoretical works on generative modeling algorithms.
sections.text: Recent works ( Fukumizu et al., 2024 ; Su et al., 2025a ; Su et al., 2025b ) study statistical convergence rates for variants of flow matching. In particular, Fukumizu et al. (2024) shows that flow matching achieves near-optimal rates in the p p -Wasserstein distance, comparable to diffusion models. However, their estimator is not neural-network-based, whereas neural networks are the primary object of study in our work. Su et al. (2025a) ; Su et al. (2025b) investigate the learning error of variants of neural-network-based flow matching, but their analysis focuses on the theoretical limits of certain neural network classes and does not address achievability by a concrete optimization procedure. In contrast, the neural network solution we study is achievable via gradient descent with polynomial-time complexity. Han et al. (2024) analyzes optimization and generalization for score matching in diffusion models using shallow neural networks. Their work does not provide distributional guarantees for samples generated from the learned score. Moreover, their two-layer network treats only the first layer weights { 𝐰 r } r ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{w}_{r}\}_{r\in[n]} as trainable parameters, whereas our analysis allows weights from both the first and second layers (a.k.a. { 𝐚 r } r ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{a}_{r}\}_{r\in[n]} and { 𝐰 r } r ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{w}_{r}\}_{r\in[n]} ) to be trainable. This distinction substantially complicates the analysis and renders several arguments in Han et al. (2024) inapplicable in our setting. Overall, much of the existing theory for flow matching is largely algorithmically agnostic, leaving a gap between statistical guarantees and practical learning procedures with polynomial-time complexity. In comparison, our analysis provides performance guarantees for gradient descent and bridges this gap by establishing algorithmic achievability.

sections.heading: Convergence and generalization guarantees for overparameterized neural networks.
sections.text: A substantial body of work studies training dynamics and generalization in the overparameterized regime. Part of our analysis is motivated by recent advances connecting trained overparameterized neural networks to the neural tangent kernel (NTK) ( Jacot et al., 2018 ) . In particular, a series of works establish convergence guarantees for gradient descent when training neural networks in the NTK regime ( Li and Liang, 2018 ; Du et al., 2019b ; Allen-Zhu et al., 2019b ; Du et al., 2019a ; Chizat et al., 2019 ; Zou et al., 2019 ; Zou and Gu, 2019 ; Lee et al., 2019 ) . Closely related studies also develop NTK-based generalization bounds for overparameterized neural networks ( Allen-Zhu et al., 2019a ; Arora et al., 2019a ; Arora et al., 2019b ; Cao and Gu, 2019 ; Ji and Telgarsky, 2020 ; Chen et al., 2021 ) . Another line of work leverages mean-field techniques to analyze the training of overparameterized shallow networks ( Mei et al., 2018 ; Chizat and Bach, 2018 ; Mei et al., 2019 ; Wei et al., 2019 ) , deep networks ( Lu et al., 2020 ; Fang et al., 2021 ; Ding et al., 2021 ; Ding et al., 2022 ) , and transformers ( Gao et al., 2024 ) . While these studies offer valuable insights and theoretical tools for deep learning, they are largely developed for standard supervised learning settings. In comparison, our work studied the generative modeling problem.

sections.heading: 3 Major Results
sections.text: This section presents the formal statements of the main results summarized in Section 1 . In Section 3.1 , we provide additional details on the problem formulation, key definitions, and the assumptions used throughout this work. In Section 3.2 , we state our three main theorems.

sections.heading: 3.1 Preliminaries, Definitions, and Assumptions
sections.text: In this section we begin by introducing the problem setup and some preliminaries. Then we introduce the assumptions made in this work.

sections.heading: 3.1.1 Problem Setup.
sections.text: In the generative modeling problem, we are given a dataset { 𝐱 1 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{1,i}\}_{i\in[n]} consisting of n n data points in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , assumed to be drawn from a high-dimensional distribution ℙ 1 \mathbb{P}_{1} . The goal is to generate additional samples 𝐱 ^ 1 \widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{1} whose distribution is close to ℙ 1 \mathbb{P}_{1} using { 𝐱 1 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{1,i}\}_{i\in[n]} . We assume that the 𝐱 1 , i \mathbf{x}_{1,i} are i.i.d.

sections.heading: Flow Matching.
sections.text: Flow matching is a state-of-the-art approach to generative modeling. It enables sampling without explicitly estimating the target distribution ℙ 1 \mathbb{P}_{1} . Instead, it specifies a path of intermediate distributions that connects a tractable, easy-to-sample base distribution ℙ 0 \mathbb{P}_{0} (e.g., a Gaussian) to the target data distribution ℙ 1 \mathbb{P}_{1} . Concretely, one draws a collection of i.i.d. samples { 𝐱 0 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{0,i}\}_{i\in[n]} from ℙ 0 \mathbb{P}_{0} as source data. The objective of flow matching is to learn a mapping 𝐮 \mathbf{u} that satisfies 𝐮 ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 ) ∼ ℙ 1 \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}_{0})\sim\mathbb{P}_{1} given 𝐱 0 ∼ ℙ 0 \mathbf{x}_{0}\sim\mathbb{P}_{0} through interpolating the two datasets { 𝐱 0 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{0,i}\}_{i\in[n]} and { 𝐱 1 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{1,i}\}_{i\in[n]} as 𝐮 ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 , i ) = 𝐱 1 , i \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}_{0,i})=\mathbf{x}_{1,i} , ∀ i ∈ [ n ] \forall i\in[n] . (3) Algorithm 1 Data generating procedure 1: input: number of samples n n , dataset { 𝐱 1 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{1,i}\}_{i\in[n]} 2: for i = 1 , 2 , … , n i=1,2,\ldots,n do 3: Sample τ i ∼ Uniform ⁡ ( [ 0 , 1 ] ) \tau_{i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform([0,1])} 4: Sample 𝐱 0 , i ∼ ℙ ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 | 𝐱 1 , i ) \mathbf{x}_{0,i}\sim\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{x}_{0}|\mathbf{x}_{1,i}) 5: Compute 𝐱 τ , i = σ τ i ⋅ 𝐱 0 , i + μ τ i ⋅ 𝐱 1 , i \mathbf{x}_{\tau,i}=\sigma_{\tau_{i}}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{0,i}+\mu_{\tau_{i}}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{1,i} 6: end for 7: return { ( τ i , 𝐱 τ i , i , 𝐱 0 , i ) } i = 1 n \{(\tau_{i},\mathbf{x}_{\tau_{i},i},\mathbf{x}_{0,i})\}_{i=1}^{n} Remark 1 . The flow matching pipeline considered in this work comprises two components: Algorithm 1 specifies the data generation procedure, and Algorithm 2 specifies the corresponding learning and sampling procedure. A key methodological choice in Algorithm 1 is that we draw the source sample 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} from the conditional distribution ℙ ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 ∣ 𝐱 1 ) \mathbb{P}(\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1}) , rather than from its marginal ℙ 0 \mathbb{P}_{0} as is customary in standard flow matching formulations ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) . This conditional coupling is adopted for theoretical reasons: it renders the population-level objective identifiable, in the sense that the target conditional velocity field 𝐯 τ \mathbf{v}_{\tau} is the unique minimizer of the expected loss. By contrast, the prevailing practice of sampling { 𝐱 0 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{0,i}\}_{i\in[n]} independently from ℙ 0 \mathbb{P}_{0} and pairing them with { 𝐱 1 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{1,i}\}_{i\in[n]} via an arbitrary coupling admits a continuum of population minimizers, which precludes meaningful approximation guarantees for the learned velocity field.

sections.heading: 3.1.2 Assumptions.
sections.text: We introduce a few assumptions considered in this work. Assumption 1 (Weak) . We assume that the distribution of ℙ 1 \mathbb{P}_{1} is sub-Gaussian with 𝔼 ⁡ [ exp ⁡ ( 𝒕 ⊤ ​ 𝐱 1 , i ) ] ≤ exp ⁡ ( C ​ d ​ ‖ 𝒕 ‖ 2 2 / 2 ) . \mathbb{E}[\exp(\bm{t}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{1,i})]\leq\exp\left({Cd\|\bm{t}\|_{2}^{2}}/{2}\right). sections.heading: 3.2 Main Theorems
sections.text: This section presents the main results of this work. We state three theorems addressing (1) approximation guarantees for gradient descent, (2) generalization bounds for conditional velocity field learning, and (3) sampling error bounds. These results answer the three questions posed in the Introduction , respectively.

sections.heading: The Approximation Bound.
sections.text: We introduce the following new notations 𝒖 i ( t ) := 𝒇 𝜽 ( t ) ​ ( 𝐱 τ i , τ i , 𝐱 0 , i ) , 𝐯 i := 𝐯 τ i ​ ( 𝐱 τ i | 𝐱 1 , i ) , Δ ( t ) := 𝑼 ( t ) − 𝑽 , \displaystyle\bm{u}_{i}^{(t)}:=\bm{f}_{\bm{\theta}^{(t)}}\left(\mathbf{x}_{\tau_{i}},\tau_{i},\mathbf{x}_{0,i}\right),\quad\mathbf{v}_{i}:=\mathbf{v}_{\tau_{i}}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau_{i}}|\mathbf{x}_{1,i}),\quad\Delta^{(t)}:=\bm{U}^{(t)}-\bm{V}, 𝑼 ( t ) := [ 𝒖 1 ( t ) , ⊤ , … , 𝒖 n ( t ) , ⊤ ] ⊤ , 𝑽 := [ 𝐯 1 ⊤ , … ​ 𝐯 n ⊤ ] ⊤ . \displaystyle\bm{U}^{(t)}:=[\bm{u}_{1}^{(t),\top},\ldots,\bm{u}_{n}^{(t),\top}]^{\top},\quad\bm{V}:=[\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top},\ldots\mathbf{v}_{n}^{\top}]^{\top}. Let 𝛉 ( t ) \bm{\theta}^{(t)} being the learned parameters of the neural network with t ≥ C η ​ λ min ​ ( 𝐇 ( ∞ ) ) ​ log ⁡ n δ t\geq\frac{C}{\eta\lambda_{\min}(\bm{H}^{(\infty)})}\log\frac{n}{\delta} iterations of training. Our generalization bound implies that, with high probability, there exists a neural network produced by gradient descent whose generalization loss scales as d n ​ log ⁡ ( n / δ ) \sqrt{\frac{d}{n}\log(n/\delta)} . This rate is analogous to the minimax rates that arise in many high-dimensional regression problems ( Wainwright, 2019 ) . A key technical difficulty is that our generalization error is measured in an L 2 L_{2} norm and the associated loss is unbounded, which falls outside the scope of many standard learning-theoretic tools developed for bounded losses. To address this issue, we develop a new Rademacher-complexity-based generalization bound tailored to unbounded loss functions. These techniques and the corresponding proof machinery are extensively discussed in Section B . To facilitate the generalization bound given by Theorem 3.3 , we introduce a new generalization bound for multi-task learning with unbounded losses. (2016) R 𝐱 ​ ( F ) = 1 n ​ 𝔼 ​ [ sup f ∈ F ∑ i = 1 n ∑ j = 1 d ϵ i ​ j ​ f j ​ ( 𝐱 ~ i ) | { 𝐱 ~ i } i ∈ [ n ] ] , \displaystyle\pazocal{R}_{\mathbf{x}}(\pazocal{F})=\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\sup_{f\in\pazocal{F}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\epsilon_{ij}f_{j}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{i})\bigg|\{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}\bigg], where ϵ i ​ j \epsilon_{ij} s are i.i.d. random sign. sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: We discuss the limitations and a few open questions for future investigation. The first question we did not manage to answer is the sharpness of the bound given by the theorems in Section 3. To address this issue, one may need to construct a few example distributions that are hard to learn with flow matching algorithms. Another direction is that we only consider a two-layer neural network, and it is worth investigating whether deeper neural networks might exhibit different convergence behavior and distribution-learning properties. Finally, we only consider the simple gradient descent algorithm. In the real world applications, researchers normally utilize stochastic gradient descent methods or the Adam optimizer for optimizing deep neural networks. Whether these methods can yield similar results, or even provide better convergence guarantees for the learning procedure, is also worth exploring.

sections.heading: Appendix B Generalization Analysis
sections.text: This section discusses some intermediate results in the proof of the generalization bound given by Theorem 3.3 . Consider a class of functions F \pazocal{F} containing functions ℝ d → ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} . The following empirical multi-task Rademacher complexity is introduced by Maurer et al. [2016] R 𝐱 ​ ( F ) = 1 n ​ 𝔼 ​ [ sup f ∈ F ∑ i = 1 n ∑ j = 1 d ϵ i ​ j ​ f j ​ ( 𝐱 ~ i ) | { 𝐱 ~ i } i ∈ [ n ] ] , \displaystyle\pazocal{R}_{\mathbf{x}}(\pazocal{F})=\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\sup_{f\in\pazocal{F}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\epsilon_{ij}f_{j}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{i})\bigg|\{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}\bigg], where ϵ i ​ j \epsilon_{ij} s are i.i.d. random sign. This complexity has been widely used in multi-task learning settings, where the output of the learning algorithm is multivariate. We also note that in related work Han et al. [2024] , the authors construct a coupling between kernel-based regression and neural networks, and derive generalization bounds by leveraging existing results for kernel-based regression. In contrast, we adopt a different approach by directly upper bounding the empirical Rademacher complexity of the neural network class. We establish the following lemma, which provides generalization bounds for unbounded losses and complements the bounded-loss results in [ Maurer, 2016 ] . Lemma B.1 . Suppose the loss function ℓ ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) \ell(\cdot,\cdot) satisfies 𝔼 ⁡ [ sup 𝐟 ∈ F cosh ⁡ ( λ ​ ℓ ​ ( f ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) , y ) ) ] ≤ exp ⁡ ( 1 2 ​ σ 2 ​ λ 2 ) \mathbb{E}[\sup_{\bm{f}\in\pazocal{F}}\cosh(\lambda\ell(f(\mathbf{x}),y))]\leq\exp(\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}\lambda^{2}) for all λ ∈ ℝ \lambda\in\mathbb{R} . And ℓ ⁡ ( f ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) , 𝐲 ) \ell(f(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{y}) is ρ \rho -Lipschitz in the first argument in Euclidean norm. Then with probability at least 1 − δ 1-\delta over the samples { 𝐱 i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{i\in[n]} , sup f ∈ F { 𝔼 [ ℓ ( f ( 𝐱 ) , 𝐲 ) ] \displaystyle\sup_{f\in\pazocal{F}}\Big\{\mathbb{E}[\ell(f(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{y})] − 1 n ∑ i = 1 n ℓ ( f ( 𝐱 i ) , 𝐲 i ) } ≤ 2 ρ R 𝐱 ( F ) + σ 2 ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / δ ) n . \displaystyle-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(f(\mathbf{x}_{i}),\mathbf{y}_{i})\Big\}\leq 2\rho{\pazocal{R}}_{\mathbf{x}}(\pazocal{F})+\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\log(1/\delta)}{n}}. Remark 7 . We note that the condition of 𝔼 ⁡ [ sup 𝒇 ∈ F cosh ⁡ ( λ ​ ℓ ​ ( f ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) , y ) ) ] ≤ exp ⁡ ( 1 2 ​ σ 2 ​ λ 2 ) \mathbb{E}[\sup_{\bm{f}\in\pazocal{F}}\cosh(\lambda\ell(f(\mathbf{x}),y))]\leq\exp(\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}\lambda^{2}) entails a strong tail control for the supremum of the stochastic process ℓ ⁡ ( f ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) , y ) \ell(f(\mathbf{x}),y) . A closely related condition appears in Meir and Zhang [2003] , where the authors study the standard univariate setting. Our bound extends their analysis to the multi-task learning regime. We next elaborate on the choice of the function class F \pazocal{F} . Since the class of neural networks is inherently unbounded, it is essential to exploit additional structure induced by the gradient descent dynamics. In particular, Lemma A.2 suggests that, with high probability, the parameter deviations ‖ 𝐚 r ( t ) − 𝐚 r ( 0 ) ‖ 2 \|\mathbf{a}_{r}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}_{r}^{(0)}\|_{2} and ‖ 𝐰 r ( t ) − 𝐰 r ( 0 ) ‖ 2 \|\mathbf{w}_{r}^{(t)}-\mathbf{w}_{r}^{(0)}\|_{2} remain small throughout optimization. Motivated by this observation, we consider the following restricted class: F R 𝐚 , R 𝐰 : \displaystyle\pazocal{F}_{R_{\mathbf{a}},R_{\mathbf{w}}}: = { { 𝐰 r } r ∈ [ m ] , { 𝐚 r } r ∈ [ m ] : ( ∑ r = 1 m ∥ 𝐰 r − 𝐰 r ( 0 ) ∥ 2 2 ) 1 / 2 ≤ R 𝐰 , \displaystyle=\Big\{\{\mathbf{w}_{r}\}_{r\in[m]},\{\mathbf{a}_{r}\}_{r\in[m]}:\Big(\sum_{r=1}^{m}\|\mathbf{w}_{r}-\mathbf{w}_{r}^{(0)}\|_{2}^{2}\Big)^{{1}/{2}}\leq R_{\mathbf{w}}, ( ∑ r = 1 m ∥ 𝐚 r − 𝐚 r ( 0 ) ∥ 2 2 ) 1 / 2 ≤ R 𝐚 , ∀ r ∈ [ m ] } . \displaystyle\Big(\sum_{r=1}^{m}\|\mathbf{a}_{r}-\mathbf{a}_{r}^{(0)}\|_{2}^{2}\Big)^{{1}/{2}}\leq R_{\mathbf{a}},\forall r\in[m]\Big\}. We emphasize that F R 𝐚 , R 𝐰 \pazocal{F}_{R_{\mathbf{a}},R_{\mathbf{w}}} imposes simultaneous control over all network weights, rather than bounding an individual parameter vector 𝐚 r \mathbf{a}_{r} as in Lemma A.2 . With this restriction, the analysis decomposes into three components: (1) upper bounding the empirical Rademacher complexity R 𝐱 ​ ( F ) \pazocal{R}_{\mathbf{x}}(\pazocal{F}) for the class F R 𝐰 , R 𝐚 \pazocal{F}_{R_{\mathbf{w}},R_{\mathbf{a}}} ; (2) establishing that the defining constraints of F R 𝐚 , R 𝐰 \pazocal{F}_{R_{\mathbf{a}},R_{\mathbf{w}}} hold with high probability along the gradient descent trajectory; and (3) upper bounding the sub-Gaussian parameter σ \sigma and verifying that the moment condition in Lemma 3.4 is satisfied for the neural networks under consideration. To bound the Rademacher complexity, we first establish the following lemma. Lemma B.2 . Under assumptions 1 , 3 , and 4 , given κ = O ⁡ ( λ 0 ​ δ n ) \kappa=O(\frac{\lambda_{0}\delta}{n}) and m = κ − 2 ​ poly ​ ( n , d , δ − 1 , λ min − 1 ​ ( 𝐇 ( ∞ ) ) ) m=\kappa^{-2}\text{poly}(n,d,\delta^{-1},\lambda_{\min}^{-1}(\bm{H}^{(\infty)})) the empirical Rademacher complexity of class F R 𝐚 , R 𝐰 \pazocal{F}_{R_{\mathbf{a}},R_{\mathbf{w}}} is bounded as follows with probability at least 1 − δ 1-\delta over the training samples and the initialization of the network parameters, R ⁡ ( F R 𝐰 , R 𝐚 ) \displaystyle\pazocal{R}(\pazocal{F}_{R_{\mathbf{w}},R_{\mathbf{a}}}) ≤ 2 ​ 𝑽 ​ 𝑯 ( ∞ ) , − 1 ​ 𝑽 ⊤ ​ d ​ log 2 ​ ( n / δ ) n + C ⋅ poly ​ ( n , λ min − 1 ​ ( 𝑯 ( ∞ ) ) , d , 1 / δ ) m 1 / 4 ​ κ 1 / 2 . \displaystyle\leq 2\sqrt{\bm{V}\bm{H}^{(\infty),-1}\bm{V}^{\top}}\sqrt{\frac{d\log^{2}(n/\delta)}{n}}+\frac{C\cdot\text{poly}(n,\lambda_{\min}^{-1}(\bm{H}^{(\infty)}),d,1/\delta)}{m^{1/4}\kappa^{1/2}}. Remark 8 . In Lemma B.2 , we show that the empirical Rademacher complexity admits an upper bound in terms of 𝑽 ​ 𝑯 ( ∞ ) , − 1 ​ 𝑽 ⊤ \sqrt{\bm{V}\bm{H}^{(\infty),-1}\bm{V}^{\top}} , which is itself bounded by B 0 B_{0} with high probability. A related bound is obtained in Arora et al. [2019a] for the univariate setting where only the 𝐰 \mathbf{w} parameters are trainable. sections.heading: Appendix G Additional Experimental Details
sections.text: This appendix provides the sliced Wasserstein-1 estimator (Appendix G.1 ), the complete per-cell gradient-descent trajectories for the simulation experiments (Appendices G.2 – G.3 ), and the training dynamics and full reconstruction grids for the real-world experiments (Appendix G.4 ). All experiments were conducted on Princeton University’s HPC cluster using NVIDIA H200 GPU nodes. The simulation experiments (Experiments 1 − 2 1-2 ) consist of 1,500 1,500 training runs (a 5 × 3 × 10 5\times 3\times 10 grid of network width, step size, and dimension, replicated over 10 10 random seeds), parallelized across 10 10 SLURM array tasks each allocated 1 1 GPU, 1 1 CPU core, and 16 16 GB RAM; total wall-clock time was under 10 GPU-hours. The real-data experiments (MNIST and Fashion-MNIST) consist of 12 12 training runs per dataset, parallelized across 4 4 array tasks each allocated 1 1 GPU, 4 4 CPU cores, and 32 32 GB RAM; total wall-clock time was under 2 2 GPU-hours per dataset.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2606.10089v1 [cs.LG] 08 Jun 2026 A Theory on Flow Matching with Neural Networks Yihan He Qishuo Yin Yuan Cao Jianqing Fan Han Liu May 7, 2026 Abstract In this work, we develop theoretical foundation for flow matching with neural-network–parameterized conditional velocity fields. We establish convergence guarantees for gradient descent in the over-parameterized 2-layered ReLU neural network regime. We derive generalization bounds for the conditional velocity-field matching objective. Building on these results, we provide Wasserstein-distance guarantees for the samples generated by the induced flow. Our analysis is based on generalization bound for multi-task representation learning with unbounded losses, which may be of independent interest beyond flow-based generative modeling. These theoretical results are validated through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world image benchmarks. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal Contribution. 1 1 footnotetext: Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA. Emails: {yihan.he, qy1448, jqfan}@princeton.edu . 2 2 footnotetext: The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong. Email: yuancao@hku.hk . 3 3 footnotetext: Northwestern University, Evanston, IL, USA. Email: hanliu@eecs.northwestern.edu . 1 Introduction Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2022 ) has emerged as a state-of-the-art approach within diffusion-based generative modeling for learning and sampling high-dimensional data, including images ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , and has been applied broadly across a range of other domains ( Lipman et al., 2024b ) . Flow matching is attractive in part because it cleanly separates three design choices: (i) the path of intermediate distributions (e.g., linear interpolation in data space / straight-line couplings in rectified flow ( Liu et al., 2022 ) , variance-preserving/variance-exploding diffusion schedules ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) , or transport maps motivated by optimal transport ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) ), (ii) the target velocity associated with that path ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) , and (iii) the numerical solver used at sampling time ( Chen et al., 2018 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . This modularity has led to a growing ecosystem of variants, including conditional flow matching constructions that leverage conditional distributions and couplings to define tractable target velocities ( Tong et al., 2024 ) . Empirically, these methods have been applied to high-dimensional generation tasks such as images, audio, and video ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Lipman et al., 2024a ; Guan et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2025 ) , and have also been used for conditional generation and editing, where one integrates an ODE while enforcing constraints (e.g., classifier guidance, inverse problems, or conditioning variables) ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Ho and Salimans, 2022 ; Song et al., 2022 ; Chung et al., 2023 ) . Beyond generation, learned continuous-time transports are increasingly used as primitives for data interpolation, domain translation, and simulation of complex dynamical systems ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Tong et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2018 ) . Despite this empirical success, a theoretical understanding of flow matching remains incomplete. There are three intertwined sources of error that ultimately determine the quality of generated samples: (1) optimization error from training neural networks with nonconvex objectives using first-order methods, (2) statistical error from learning the velocity field from finitely many samples, and (3) sampling error from approximating the continuous-time dynamics with a neural network learned velocity field. Hence, the questions that we address in this work can be summarized as follows: 1. What is the convergence guarantee for the neural network training with gradient descent ? 2. What is the generalization guarantee for the velocity field matching ? 3. What is the distributional guarantee for samples generated by neural-network-based flow matching? Contributions. To address the three questions above, we summarize our main contributions as follows. 1. We establish convergence guarantees for approximating high-dimensional conditional velocity fields using gradient-descent-trained two-layer neural networks. Our analysis connects the training dynamics to the neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime ( Du et al., 2018 ; Jacot et al., 2018 ) and addresses the challenges posed by high dimensionality, including regimes where the data dimension d d is of the same order as the sample size n n . 2. We derive L 2 L_{2} statistical error bounds for the velocity field learning problem by introducing a general high-dimensional multi-task learning generalization bound for unbounded losses. This result complements existing representation learning theory ( Maurer, 2016 ; Maurer et al., 2016 ) and may be of independent interest. 3. We provide sampling error guarantees for flow matching in Wasserstein distance. The proof combines a geometric lemma that upgrades L 1 L_{1} control to L ∞ L_{\infty} control on a compact high-dimensional subset with a refined analysis of the induced ODE dynamics. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first sampling error guarantee for gradient-descent-trained, neural-network-based flow matching algorithms. 4. Our theoretical results are complemented by numerical experiments on both the synthetic and real-world images that validate the convergence and sampling error bounds. These experiments provide insights into the practical implications of our theoretical findings and highlight potential avenues for future research. Organization. The remainder of this work is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work and positions our contributions relative to existing literature. Section 3 introduces the main definitions and summarizes our results. Section 4 reports numerical experiments that complement the theoretical analysis. Finally, Section 5 discusses limitations and directions for future work. 2 Related Works Our work is closely related to two branches of recent theoretical research on generative modeling and overparameterized neural networks. In the following, we first review recent theoretical developments for flow matching models, and then discuss the techniques most directly related to those used in this work. Theoretical works on generative modeling algorithms. Recent works ( Fukumizu et al., 2024 ; Su et al., 2025a ; Su et al., 2025b ) study statistical convergence rates for variants of flow matching. In particular, Fukumizu et al. (2024) shows that flow matching achieves near-optimal rates in the p p -Wasserstein distance, comparable to diffusion models. However, their estimator is not neural-network-based, whereas neural networks are the primary object of study in our work. Su et al. (2025a) ; Su et al. (2025b) investigate the learning error of variants of neural-network-based flow matching, but their analysis focuses on the theoretical limits of certain neural network classes and does not address achievability by a concrete optimization procedure. In contrast, the neural network solution we study is achievable via gradient descent with polynomial-time complexity. Han et al. (2024) analyzes optimization and generalization for score matching in diffusion models using shallow neural networks. Their work does not provide distributional guarantees for samples generated from the learned score. Moreover, their two-layer network treats only the first layer weights { 𝐰 r } r ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{w}_{r}\}_{r\in[n]} as trainable parameters, whereas our analysis allows weights from both the first and second layers (a.k.a. { 𝐚 r } r ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{a}_{r}\}_{r\in[n]} and { 𝐰 r } r ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{w}_{r}\}_{r\in[n]} ) to be trainable. This distinction substantially complicates the analysis and renders several arguments in Han et al. (2024) inapplicable in our setting. Overall, much of the existing theory for flow matching is largely algorithmically agnostic, leaving a gap between statistical guarantees and practical learning procedures with polynomial-time complexity. In comparison, our analysis provides performance guarantees for gradient descent and bridges this gap by establishing algorithmic achievability. Convergence and generalization guarantees for overparameterized neural networks. A substantial body of work studies training dynamics and generalization in the overparameterized regime. Part of our analysis is motivated by recent advances connecting trained overparameterized neural networks to the neural tangent kernel (NTK) ( Jacot et al., 2018 ) . In particular, a series of works establish convergence guarantees for gradient descent when training neural networks in the NTK regime ( Li and Liang, 2018 ; Du et al., 2019b ; Allen-Zhu et al., 2019b ; Du et al., 2019a ; Chizat et al., 2019 ; Zou et al., 2019 ; Zou and Gu, 2019 ; Lee et al., 2019 ) . Closely related studies also develop NTK-based generalization bounds for overparameterized neural networks ( Allen-Zhu et al., 2019a ; Arora et al., 2019a ; Arora et al., 2019b ; Cao and Gu, 2019 ; Ji and Telgarsky, 2020 ; Chen et al., 2021 ) . Another line of work leverages mean-field techniques to analyze the training of overparameterized shallow networks ( Mei et al., 2018 ; Chizat and Bach, 2018 ; Mei et al., 2019 ; Wei et al., 2019 ) , deep networks ( Lu et al., 2020 ; Fang et al., 2021 ; Ding et al., 2021 ; Ding et al., 2022 ) , and transformers ( Gao et al., 2024 ) . While these studies offer valuable insights and theoretical tools for deep learning, they are largely developed for standard supervised learning settings. In comparison, our work studied the generative modeling problem. 3 Major Results This section presents the formal statements of the main results summarized in Section 1 . In Section 3.1 , we provide additional details on the problem formulation, key definitions, and the assumptions used throughout this work. In Section 3.2 , we state our three main theorems. Notations. Throughout, we use the following notation conventions. Vector-valued quantities are denoted by boldfaced characters. We write [ n ] := 1 , … , n [n]:={1,\ldots,n} and [ i : j ] := i , i + 1 , … , j [i:j]:={i,i+1,\ldots,j} for i < j i<j . Universal constants are denoted by C C and may change from line to line. For a vector 𝒗 \bm{v} , we denote its ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm by ‖ 𝒗 ‖ 2 \|\bm{v}\|_{2} . For a matrix 𝑨 ∈ ℝ m × n \bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , we denote its operator norm by ‖ 𝑨 ‖ 2 := sup 𝒗 ∈ 𝕊 n − 1 ‖ 𝑨 ​ 𝒗 ‖ 2 \|\bm{A}\|_{2}:=\sup_{\bm{v}\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\|\bm{A}\bm{v}\|_{2} . We use 𝟙 \mathbbm{1} to denote the indicator function. 3.1 Preliminaries, Definitions, and Assumptions In this section we begin by introducing the problem setup and some preliminaries. Then we introduce the assumptions made in this work. 3.1.1 Problem Setup. In the generative modeling problem, we are given a dataset { 𝐱 1 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{1,i}\}_{i\in[n]} consisting of n n data points in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , assumed to be drawn from a high-dimensional distribution ℙ 1 \mathbb{P}_{1} . The goal is to generate additional samples 𝐱 ^ 1 \widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{1} whose distribution is close to ℙ 1 \mathbb{P}_{1} using { 𝐱 1 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{1,i}\}_{i\in[n]} . We assume that the 𝐱 1 , i \mathbf{x}_{1,i} are i.i.d. Flow Matching. Flow matching is a state-of-the-art approach to generative modeling. It enables sampling without explicitly estimating the target distribution ℙ 1 \mathbb{P}_{1} . Instead, it specifies a path of intermediate distributions that connects a tractable, easy-to-sample base distribution ℙ 0 \mathbb{P}_{0} (e.g., a Gaussian) to the target data distribution ℙ 1 \mathbb{P}_{1} . Concretely, one draws a collection of i.i.d. samples { 𝐱 0 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{0,i}\}_{i\in[n]} from ℙ 0 \mathbb{P}_{0} as source data. The objective of flow matching is to learn a mapping 𝐮 \mathbf{u} that satisfies 𝐮 ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 ) ∼ ℙ 1 \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}_{0})\sim\mathbb{P}_{1} given 𝐱 0 ∼ ℙ 0 \mathbf{x}_{0}\sim\mathbb{P}_{0} through interpolating the two datasets { 𝐱 0 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{0,i}\}_{i\in[n]} and { 𝐱 1 , i } i ∈ [ n ] \{\mathbf{x}_{1,i}\}_{i\in[n]} as 𝐮 ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 , i ) = 𝐱 1 , i \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}_{0,i})=\mathbf{x}_{1,i} , ∀ i ∈ [ n ] \forall i\in[n] . The flow matching algorithm learns a transport path between 𝐱 0 , i \mathbf{x}_{0,i} and 𝐱 1 , i \mathbf{x}_{1,i} , i ∈ [ n ] i\in[n] by constructing a conditional velocity field 𝐯 τ ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{v}_{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that, for all τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \tau\in[0,1] , d ​ 𝐱 τ d ​ τ = 𝐯 τ ​ ( 𝐱 τ | 𝐱 0 ) := σ τ ′ ⋅ 𝐱 0 + μ τ ′ μ τ ​ ( 𝐱 τ − σ τ ​ 𝐱 0 ) , \displaystyle\frac{d\mathbf{x}_{\tau}}{d\tau}=\mathbf{v}_{\tau}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}|\mathbf{x}_{0}):=\sigma_{\tau}^{\prime}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{0}+\frac{\mu_{\tau}^{\prime}}{\mu_{\tau}}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau}-\sigma_{\tau}\mathbf{x}_{0}), (1) where σ \sigma and μ \mu satisfying σ 0 = μ 1 = 1 \sigma_{0}=\mu_{1}=1 , σ 1 = μ 0 = 0 \sigma_{1}=\mu_{0}=0 are scalar functions with derivatives σ ′ \sigma^{\prime} and μ ′ \mu^{\prime} , respectively. We emphasize that the conditional velocity field 𝐯 \mathbf{v} also depends on 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} and τ \tau . Under this parametrization, the target mapping 𝐮 \mathbf{u} can be obtained by solving the ODE in ( 1 ) to produce 𝐱 1 \mathbf{x}_{1} from the initial condition 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} . In practice ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Lipman et al., 2024a ) , the velocity field 𝐯 τ \mathbf{v}_{\tau} is frequently represented by a neural network. In this work, we consider the following overparameterized two-layer neural network: 𝒇 𝜽 ​ ( 𝐱 τ , τ , 𝐱 0 ) = 1 m ​ ∑ r = 1 m 𝐚 r ​ σ ​ ( 𝐰 r ⊤ ​ [ 𝐱 τ ⊤ , τ , 𝐱 0 ⊤ ] ⊤ ) \displaystyle\bm{f}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau},\tau,\mathbf{x}_{0})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\sum_{r=1}^{m}\mathbf{a}_{r}\sigma\left(\mathbf{w}_{r}^{\top}[\mathbf{x}_{\tau}^{\top},\tau,\mathbf{x}_{0}^{\top}]^{\top}\right) where m m denotes the width of the neural network.
